props.title: Pygmalion
props.initialSlug: Professor transforms cockney flower girl into lady

sections.content: Pygmalion (1938) stands as the definitive screen adaptation of George Bernard Shaw's razor-sharp social satire, laying the groundwork for My Fair Lady (1964). Anthony Asquith and Leslie Howard's direction captures Shaw's biting commentary on class, language, and identity through the story of phonetics professor Henry Higgins transforming cockney flower girl Eliza Doolittle. Wendy Hiller's breakthrough performance as Eliza sets the template for social mobility tales, while Leslie Howard's arrogant Higgins established the archetypal mentor-student dynamic that influenced films like The King's Speech (2010) and Dead Poets Society (1989).

sections.content: The film's technical achievements in capturing British class distinctions through accent and costume influenced decades of social commentary cinema. Room at the Top (1959) and Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1960) built on Pygmalion's examination of class mobility, while modern films like Trading Places (1983) and Pretty Woman (1990) reworked its transformation narrative for new audiences. The sharp dialogue and wit of Shaw's original text translates remarkably well to screen, proving more naturalistic than many contemporary productions. SUBHEAD: Class and Social Transformation in Cinema

Pygmalion's DNA runs through countless films exploring class, education, and personal transformation. Educating Rita (1983) directly channels its spirit in the story of a working-class hairdresser pursuing higher education. She's All That (1999) and Miss Congeniality (2000) adapted the makeover elements for teen and comedy audiences. The mentor-student relationship between Higgins and Eliza influenced everything from To Sir, With Love (1967) to Good Will Hunting (1997), though modern takes typically avoid Higgins' patronizing attitudes.
